concepts.name: The Dagh (Branding) System and its Military Significance
key_dimensions: Revival and refinement of Alauddin Khalji's branding system by Sher Shah
Purpose: preventing substitution of inferior horses and ensuring quality of cavalry
How it curbed corruption among military commanders (ahdis and mansabdars)
Comparison with Akbar's later adoption and modification of the same system

concepts.name: Chehra (Descriptive Roll) System
key_dimensions: Maintenance of physical descriptions of soldiers to prevent fraudulent musters
Relationship with the Dagh system as twin anti-corruption mechanisms
Distinction from Mughal Chehra practices under Akbar
Administrative significance beyond military: precedent for personnel records

concepts.name: Central Standing Army (Army of the Centre) under Direct Royal Control
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's deliberate policy of maintaining a large centrally paid and controlled army
Reduction of dependence on feudal/jagirdari contingents to prevent rebellions
Composition: cavalry, infantry, elephants, and artillery in the central force
Contrast with Sultanate-era reliance on iqta-holder military contributions

concepts.name: Cavalry Organisation: Structure, Pay, and Quality Control
key_dimensions: Cavalry as the premier arm; classification of horses and troopers
Direct payment of soldiers from the royal treasury (avoiding intermediaries)
Role of the Dagh system specifically in maintaining cavalry standards
Comparison with Mughal mansabdari cavalry obligations (sawar rank)

concepts.name: Infantry (Paidal) in Sher Shah's Army
key_dimensions: Relative importance of infantry compared to cavalry in Sur military doctrine
Role of Afghan tribal infantry and their integration into the standing army
Pay scales and equipment standardisation for infantry soldiers
Use of infantry in siege operations and garrison duties

concepts.name: War Elephants: Tactical and Symbolic Role
key_dimensions: Elephants as a distinct arm alongside cavalry and infantry
Tactical deployment in Sher Shah's key battles (Chausa, Kanauj/Bilgram)
Administrative management: separate elephant establishment and mahout corps
Symbolic significance of elephants as markers of imperial power

concepts.name: Artillery (Top-Khana) and Gunpowder Warfare
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's use of artillery inherited and developed from Babur's innovations
Role of artillery at Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540) against the Mughals
Organisational structure of the artillery department under Sur rule
Limitations of Sher Shah's artillery compared to later Mughal developments

concepts.name: Military Pay System: Direct Treasury Payment vs. Jagir Assignment
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's preference for cash payment (naqdi) over jagir assignment to soldiers
How direct payment reduced the power of intermediary commanders
Exceptions: some commanders still received jagirs; distinguishing policy from practice
Precedent this set for Akbar's later mansabdari payment reforms

concepts.name: Role of Afghan Tribal Nobility in the Military Hierarchy
key_dimensions: Tension between Sher Shah's centralising military reforms and Afghan tribal loyalties
How Sher Shah balanced co-opting Afghan chiefs while curtailing their autonomous military power
Appointment of loyal Afghan commanders vs. checks through the Dagh-Chehra system
Contrast with the Lodi Sultans' excessive dependence on Afghan tribal military power

concepts.name: Garrison and Fort System as Military Infrastructure
key_dimensions: Strategic placement of garrisons (thanas) along roads and frontiers
Integration of the road-building programme (Grand Trunk Road) with military logistics
Sarai (rest house) network's dual military and commercial function
How the fort-garrison network ensured rapid troop movement and internal security

concepts.name: Intelligence and Espionage in Sher Shah's Military System
key_dimensions: Use of spies (barids and munhiyans) for both military and administrative intelligence
Role of intelligence in Sher Shah's surprise manoeuvres (e.g., Chausa campaign)
Distinction between military intelligence gathering and administrative news reporting
Comparison with Alauddin Khalji's spy network and later Mughal intelligence systems

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Military Strategy: Defensive vs. Offensive Doctrine
key_dimensions: Use of terrain, monsoon seasons, and river systems in campaigns (Chausa example)
Preference for guerrilla and attrition tactics against Humayun's larger forces initially
Transition to conventional pitched battle when advantageous (Kanauj/Bilgram 1540)
Strategic use of diplomacy and alliance-building as force multipliers

concepts.name: Siege Warfare Capabilities and Engineering Corps
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's record in siege operations: Chunar, Raisin, Kalinjar (fatal siege)
Use of mining, artillery, and blockade techniques
Death of Sher Shah at Kalinjar (1545) as evidence of siege warfare hazards
Comparison of Sur siege techniques with Mughal siege engineering under Akbar

concepts.name: Revenue-Military Nexus: Land Revenue Reforms as a Foundation for Military Strength
key_dimensions: How the ryotwari-style land revenue reforms provided stable treasury income for military pay
Elimination of tax-farming intermediaries to maximise revenue for military expenditure
Connection between the measurement of land (Sher Shah's surveys) and military resource planning
UPSC trap: distinguishing Sher Shah's revenue reforms as a military enabler vs. purely administrative reform

concepts.name: The Ahadis (Gentlemen Troopers) and Elite Cavalry Units
key_dimensions: Ahadis as individually enrolled elite horsemen directly under royal command (pre-Akbar origin)
Role in maintaining a loyal royal household force independent of noble contingents
Pay and status distinctions between ahadis and ordinary cavalry troopers
Continuity of the ahadi institution into Akbar's Mughal military organisation

concepts.name: Command Structure: From the Sultan to the Faujdar
key_dimensions: Hierarchical chain: Sultan → central commanders → provincial faujdars → local thanedar
Role of the faujdar as the key military-administrative officer at the regional level
Accountability mechanisms: how faujdars reported to the centre and were checked
Continuity of the faujdari system into the Mughal and later Maratha administrative frameworks

concepts.name: Logistics, Supply Chain, and the Role of the Road Network
key_dimensions: Grand Trunk Road (Sadak-e-Azam) as a strategic military supply and movement corridor
Sarai network providing shelter, fodder, and provisions for marching armies
Postal relay (dak-chowki) system for rapid military communications
How superior logistics gave Sher Shah strategic mobility over his opponents

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Military Reforms as a Precedent for Akbar's Mansabdari System
key_dimensions: Specific elements Akbar borrowed: Dagh, Chehra, central army concept, direct pay
Key differences: Akbar formalised a graded numerical rank (mansab) absent in Sur system
UPSC trap: attributing the origin of Dagh-Chehra exclusively to Akbar vs. Sher Shah
Historiographical debate on the degree of continuity between Sur and Mughal military institutions

concepts.name: Treatment of Defeated Enemies and Integration into the Military
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's policy of absorbing Rajput and other non-Afghan warriors into his forces
Use of religious and ethnic diversity in the army as a tool of imperial consolidation
Contrast with purely Afghan exclusivist military policy of Lodi Sultans
How this policy of inclusion compared to Akbar's later Rajput integration strategy
